primary_claim: DSPy-based prompt optimization (GEPA) of a trusted monitor for AI control substantially improves monitor safety over manually-written baseline monitors, achieving ~90% safety at a 1% audit budget versus baseline monitors failing to exceed 70% safety.

effect.metric: safety (probability no backdoored code submitted) across audit budgets 0.5%-5%
effect.value: prompt-optimized monitor: ~90% safety at 1% audit budget vs baseline <70%; fine-tuned monitor: 85% safety at 0.5% audit budget vs ~60% for others; ControlArena basic_monitor: ~20% safety, roughly flat across budgets

contradicts_or_qualifies: ControlTax evaluation's noted limitation regarding lack of model-specific prompt optimization
stated_future_work: Does this prompt immediately work well in other settings?
How does an improved trusted monitor affect dependent protocols, like defer-to-trusted and defer-to-trusted-edit?
Could DSPy be further leveraged by composing more complex modules?
Is the comparative pairs metric the best way to train a monitor, or is there a better way?
Can DSPy prompt optimization help with other control tasks, like trusted editors or red team optimization?
limitations_stated: This initial experiment did not consider the red team's response to the optimized monitor (no adaptive red-teaming).
The experiment focused entirely on the APPS setting; it is unclear how the procedure transfers to other control settings.
Using GPT-5 as the reflection LLM for the blue team is more powerful than typical control setups allow, though this is treated as a simulation of manual prompt engineering.
Designing effective metrics with feedback turned out to be a primary difficulty, not manual prompt writing itself.
Possible collusion between the reflection LLM and an attack LLM if prompt optimization were used against a live red team in practice.
quote: The prompt-optimized monitors (green) achieve ~90% safety with a 1% audit budget, while baseline monitors fail to exceed 70% safety.
